payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: What paper and receiving objects are visibly present in the source and edited images, and does direct feature comparison establish whether an edited receiving object is a cup?
node.criteria: Pass if the images permit a grounded inventory and comparison, even if a particular identity remains unresolved. Separately report source paper and cup identification, edited paper and cup identification, and source-to-edit correspondence as established, disproved, or unresolved, with visible reasons. Inventory pass does not establish cup identity or insertion. Fail if adequate edited-image visibility positively establishes absence of the paper or any relevant receiving object. Unknown if visibility prevents a grounded inventory. A source cup does not by itself establish an edited cup, and unresolved correspondence does not prove removal.
node.binding: Inspect both images directly. First identify objects from visible structure in each image; then compare candidate counterparts using contour, proportions, opening or rim structure, enclosing walls, orientation, and other distinctive features that are actually visible. Allow source evidence to inform identity when supported by edited-image correspondence, but do not transfer source geometry into an occluded edit. Test retention, alteration, replacement, and unresolved correspondence without presupposing any of them. A color change alone neither establishes nor disproves cup identity. Describe edited paper boundaries, candidate receiving-object boundaries, overlap, and precisely which regions are obscured. Do not demand a visible interior as the sole identity test, infer insertion from a hand grip, or infer any object from the instruction alone.

node_traces.evidence: Source: a large white sheet of paper is visible beside a blue cylindrical cup; the cup has a rounded body and a clearly visible circular rim/opening facing the camera. Edited: a blue printed paper/card is held in a hand, with its boundaries visible; behind it is a reddish rounded object with a dark curved line, but the image does not show enough of its contour or structure to identify it as a cup or establish correspondence with the source cup. The paper overlaps and obscures part of that object. The images allow a grounded inventory and comparison, while edited receiving-object identity and source-to-edit correspondence remain unresolved.

Source: a large white sheet of paper is visible at left, beside a blue cylindrical vessel with enclosing walls and a broad circular rim/opening facing the camera; it is identifiable as a cup. Edited: a blue printed paper/card with visible edges is held in front of a reddish rounded object. The reddish object is partly obscured by the paper and hand; only a curved outer boundary and a dark line are visible, with no clear rim or enclosing-wall structure to establish it as a cup. The edited paper differs in appearance and shape from the source sheet, and the candidate receiving object does not visibly correspond to the source blue cup. Correspondence is unresolved; the edited image does visibly contain paper and a possible receiving object. The images allow a grounded inventory and comparison, so the inventory check passes, but cup identity and object correspondence in the edit remain unresolved.

Source: a large white sheet of paper is visible at left, beside a blue cylindrical cup lying on its side; the cup’s oval rim/opening and enclosing wall are clearly visible. Edited: a blue printed paper/card is held in a hand, with its boundaries visible except where covered by the fingers; a reddish rounded object behind it has a curved outline and a dark curved line, but its boundaries and structure are partly obscured. The edited image does not visibly establish that this object is the source cup: its visible shape differs from the source cup’s rim-and-wall structure, and correspondence is unresolved. The paper and candidate receiving object are both present in the edited image; no insertion is established.

Source: a large white sheet of paper is visible beside a blue cup lying on its side; the cup has a broad oval opening and enclosing walls. Edited: a blue printed paper/card is held in front of a reddish rounded object with a dark curved line. The paper’s outline is mostly visible, though its upper edge is partly overlapped by the hand; the reddish object is partly obscured by the paper and hand, and its visible contour does not clearly establish a cup. Direct comparison does not establish that the edited reddish object corresponds to the source cup. The images allow a grounded inventory, but edited cup identity and source-to-edit correspondence remain unresolved.

Source: a large white sheet of paper is visible at left, beside a blue cup lying on its side at right; the cup has a broad oval rim/opening and tapered enclosing walls. Edited: a blue printed paper/card is clearly visible, held by a hand, with its boundaries mostly discernible. Behind it is a reddish rounded object with a dark curved line, but the paper and framing obscure much of its contour; the visible structure does not establish that it is a cup. Direct comparison therefore does not establish whether the source cup corresponds to the edited receiving object. The images allow a grounded inventory, while edited cup identity and source-to-edit correspondence remain unresolved.

The traces show why this matters: the edited paper is held over a reddish object, but its cup identity is unresolved; some boundary maps establish it wholly in front (supporting absent), while others say the contact area is obscured and entry is unresolved. Preserve that distinction: absent requires affirmative, grounded exclusion of entry, not merely missing evidence or failure to prove completion; unresolved is appropriate when occlusion leaves entry indeterminate.
